metadata.file_name: 58. Rodriguez-Barrios et al. (2021). Bayesian Approach to Analyze Reading Comprehension: A Case Study in Elementary School Children in Mexico.pdf
metadata.title: Bayesian Approach to Analyze Reading Comprehension: A Case Study in Elementary School Children in Mexico

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a small, local elementary-school sample in Misantla, Veracruz (Mexico) and reports no complex survey design or sampling weights. The Bayesian network probabilities are estimated from observed test-result frequencies (maximum likelihood estimator) and teacher-assigned discretizations of test outcomes into categorical levels. Because the paper does not describe any ILSA-style weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures, weighting is not incorporated into the reported analysis. The analytic sample appears to be the full set of participants who completed the four reading-related tests and the teacher-assigned language/communication level, with a separate control group used for validation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement Plausible Values (PVs). Instead, it constructs a Bayesian network over discretized classroom test outcomes (learning style/pace/speed and reading comprehension) and a teacher-assigned language/communication level, so PV-based handling is not relevant. The authors state they obtained complete and sufficient data for all model variables, but they do not explicitly document a missing-data handling procedure for any potential missingness, which is a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were fifth- and sixth-grade students from Escuela Primaria General Manuel Gutiérrez Zamora in Misantla, Veracruz, Mexico, during the 2018–2019 school year. The study applied four standardized instruments (learning styles, learning pace, reading speed, reading comprehension) across groups A, B, and C in Spanish class hours over ~6 weeks. Reading speed was administered ten times and then averaged into a discrete reading-speed category; reading comprehension was administered twice. The Bayesian network was built using the resulting categorical variables, and model validation used a control group of 41 students formed from test results belonging to 5th C and 6th C.

main_findings.target_variable: Language and communication level of achievement (I–IV)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Validation (control group, n=41): precision 85.36%; confusion matrix counts reported for Levels I–IV.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using local elementary-school reading assessment data in Mexico (Grades 5–6), the study leveraged learning style (VAK), learning pace, reading speed, and two reading-comprehension test results to classify language and communication level (I–IV), finding that the Bayesian network achieved 85.36% precision in validation. This indicates that Bayesian-network-based educational technology could support teachers in identifying students’ reading comprehension levels and tailoring instruction, though the evidence is limited by a small single-school sample and the absence of PV-based ILSA scaling/weighting.

data.outcome_summary: The study develops an exploratory Bayesian network to classify elementary students’ language and communication level (Levels I–IV) using four reading-related instruments: learning style (VAK), learning pace, reading speed (discretized from words/min), and reading comprehension (two administrations). The Bayesian network structure and conditional probability tables are defined using teacher/expert judgment for the architecture and maximum-likelihood estimation from observed frequencies for the parameters. For validation, the authors report a control group of 41 students (from 5th C and 6th C) and a confusion-matrix-based precision of 85.36% across Levels I–IV. The paper does not use ILSA PVs and does not report a formal missing-data strategy beyond stating complete data for model variables, so generalizability and transparency about missingness handling are limited. The approach is predictive/classificatory rather than causal, and performance may reflect local test discretizations and teacher-assigned level definitions.
